_about: Conformance vectors for the DEVICE-SIDE http_request target guard. The server validates a URL when it is saved or sent; the player enforces it again at request time. Both answer to this file, so the door cannot be stricter than the doorman.

_threat_model.what_this_is_not: This is NOT the server's SSRF guard, and it is almost its inverse. The server's json-api data sources REFUSE private addresses, because a caller making the SERVER fetch a LAN address is reaching somewhere they could not otherwise reach. Here the private address IS the feature: the whole point is that the panel talks to the PLC, the sensor, the local Home Assistant on the shop network. Refusing RFC1918 here would delete the feature.
_threat_model.what_this_is: The request is operator-initiated by someone who already holds a 'full' token, so reaching a LAN host is not an escalation — they asked for it. The escalation this guard exists to stop is a change of KIND: turning 'make an HTTP request and give me 64KiB of the answer' into 'read a file off this device and give me 64KiB of it'. On Android that is file:// and content:// — the latter reads through content providers, which is how one app's private data is exposed to another. A scheme allowlist is the whole defence and it is not negotiable.
_threat_model.secondary: Cloud metadata endpoints. A player is normally a panel on a shop wall, but nothing stops one running on a cloud VM, and 169.254.169.254 hands out IAM credentials to anything that asks. Blocking the link-local range costs nothing real: no signage device is legitimately addressed at 169.254.x.x, because that range only appears when DHCP has FAILED.

_conventions.allow: true = the player may issue this request.
_conventions.reason: when allow is false, a stable machine-readable reason: bad_scheme | metadata_address | no_host | malformed.
_conventions.note: Hostnames are checked as written here. A hostname that RESOLVES to a blocked address is caught at request time by re-checking each resolved address — that cannot be expressed as a static vector, so it has its own unit test.
_conventions.no_host: The no_host branch is DEFENSIVE and deliberately not pinned by a vector. WHATWG URL normalises 'http:///path' to host 'path' while other parsers return an empty host; pinning either answer would make one implementation wrong without making anything safer. Both still refuse or allow consistently on every url that matters, and an empty host is refused wherever a parser reports one.
